title: State of AI Industries
dek_2026: How far AI has spread through healthcare, finance, software, retail, manufacturing, education, legal, marketing and government, what each sector spends on it, and which measured outcomes exist so far.

conventions.year_mapping: Calendar year described, except school and university surveys (HEPI, Pew teens, Gallup-Walton teachers), which are labelled by the academic year they describe, using the year in which that academic year ends: HEPI fieldwork in December 2025 describes 2025-26 and is filed under 2026. This matches the labels already used on site page 865.
conventions.single_survey_rule: Cross-sector adoption rankings use one survey at a time (Ramp, Census BTOS or Eurostat). Their levels differ by design and are never placed on one chart.
conventions.access_note: Primary sites for Eurostat, the US Census Bureau and FRED could not be fetched from this environment; their figures come from search results quoting them and from consistent secondary reporting, and are rated MEDIUM.

2024: The FDA's AI-Enabled Medical Device List counted 1,016 authorized AI devices in its 20 December 2024 update, and the September 2026 snapshot of the list attributes 235 authorizations to calendar year 2024.
The American Medical Association found that 66% of US physicians used AI in their practice in its November 2024 survey of 1,183 physicians, up from 38% in 2023.
IDC estimated that banks spent about $31.3 billion on AI in 2024, more than any other industry, with retail at about $25 billion.
Ramp's AI Index showed 36.4% of US businesses on its platform paying for AI tools in November 2024, with finance and insurance at 51.2% and information-sector firms at 65.9%.
Clio's 2024 Legal Trends Report found that 79% of legal professionals used AI, up from 19% in 2023.
2025: The FDA authorized 335 AI-enabled medical devices with 2025 decision dates, according to the September 2026 snapshot of its AI device list, 42.6% more than in 2024; other counts of the same year range from 295 to 333.

Menlo Ventures estimated in October 2025 that 22% of US healthcare organizations had implemented domain-specific AI tools, up from roughly 3% in 2024, and that healthcare AI spending reached $1.4 billion in 2025.
HEPI's survey of 1,041 UK full-time undergraduates, fielded in December 2024, found that 92% used AI in some form during the 2024-25 academic year, up from 66% a year earlier.
Eurostat reported that 19.95% of EU enterprises with 10 or more employees used AI in 2025, up from 13.5% in 2024, led by the information and communication sector at 62.52%.
Salesforce estimated that AI and agents influenced $262 billion of global online holiday sales between 1 November and 31 December 2025, about 20% of the total, up from $229 billion in 2024.
2026: Ramp's AI Index showed 55.9% of US businesses on its platform paying for AI tools in September 2026; in August, technology firms were at 80.9%, finance at 73.7%, manufacturing at 61.1% and health care at 43.4%.
The US Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey found 19.8% of US businesses using AI as of 3 May 2026, including 39.7% in the information sector and 33.9% in finance and insurance.
The American Medical Association found that 81% of US physicians used AI in their practice in a survey of 1,692 physicians fielded from 15 January to 2 February 2026, up from 66% in November 2024.
The FDA's AI-Enabled Medical Device List reached 1,614 entries in its 4 September 2026 update, covering decisions through 29 June 2026, up from 1,016 in December 2024.
Clio's 2026 Legal Trends Report found that 85% of legal professionals reported some level of AI adoption at their firms, up from 79% in 2025.

2024: In 2024 AI adoption by industry was still measured mostly in pilots and licences. Ramp's AI Index showed 36.4% of US businesses on its platform paying for an AI tool in November 2024, but the spread was wide: 65.9% of information-sector firms against 51.2% in finance and insurance. Eurostat's broader, representative count found only 13.5% of EU enterprises using AI at all, with the information and communication sector at 48.72% and every sector outside the top two below 16%. The pattern that would hold for the next two years was already visible: AI arrived first where work is digital, text-based and done at a desk.

Healthcare was the clearest case of practitioners moving ahead of their institutions. The AMA found 66% of US physicians using AI in November 2024, up from 38% a year earlier, yet Menlo Ventures estimates that only about 3% of healthcare organizations had implemented domain-specific AI tools that year. Regulators kept approving products at a steady pace: the FDA list attributes 235 AI device authorizations to 2024 and passed 1,016 cumulative entries in December, about three-quarters of them in radiology. Most clinical AI in use was imaging software and general chatbots, not autonomous decision-making.

Money followed the industries that already ran on data. IDC put banking first at about $31.3 billion of AI spending in 2024, with retail at about $25 billion; Menlo's enterprise survey found healthcare the largest buyer of vertical generative-AI software at about $500 million, followed by legal at $350 million. Measured outcomes were scarce. The strongest evidence came from controlled settings, such as the MASAI mammography trial, and from the Stanford RegLab study that found leading legal research tools hallucinating on 17-33% of queries. Sector-wide productivity or revenue effects were not yet measurable in any public dataset.
2025: In 2025 broad adoption numbers stopped being the main story, because almost every survey of large organizations reported majority use. McKinsey's survey found 88% of organizations using AI in at least one function, and Eurostat's count of EU enterprises rose to 19.95%, with the information and communication sector at 62.52% and professional services at 40.43%. Ramp's paid-adoption index ended the year at 46.6%, after a flat autumn. The gap between information-heavy industries and the rest widened in absolute terms, even as Ramp's November 2025 data showed adoption rising in retail, construction and manufacturing while finance and technology dipped slightly.

Healthcare became the fastest-moving regulated sector. The FDA list records 335 AI device authorizations with 2025 decision dates, a record and 42.6% more than 2024 on the same snapshot, although other counts of the year range from 295 to 333 depending on method. Menlo Ventures found 22% of healthcare organizations had implemented domain-specific AI tools, around seven times the 2024 level, and put healthcare AI spending at $1.4 billion. Its separate enterprise survey put healthcare at $1.5 billion, 43% of all vertical generative-AI spend. Ambient scribes were the most visible deployment.

Education and the professions showed the same split between individual and institutional use. HEPI found 92% of UK undergraduates using AI, but only 23% said their university provided AI tools. Gallup and the Walton Family Foundation found 60% of US teachers had used AI in the 2024-25 school year and 32% weekly. Clio's legal adoption measure held at 79%. In software, Stack Overflow found 78% of developers using AI tools while trust in their accuracy fell to 33%, and METR's randomized trial found experienced developers 19% slower with early-2025 tools.
2026: By late 2026 a majority of US businesses on Ramp's platform paid for AI: 55.9% in September, with technology firms at about 80% and finance at 73.7%. The Census Bureau's representative survey shows a lower level, 19.8% as of May 2026, because it counts AI use across all employer businesses rather than subscriptions among Ramp's tech-leaning customers. Both surveys rank sectors the same way: information first, then professional services and finance, with retail, accommodation and food services, and construction at the bottom. On Ramp's August data the top sector is about 2.4 times the bottom one.

Healthcare's practitioner adoption is now near the level of the most digital industries. The AMA found 81% of US physicians using AI in early 2026, and the FDA list reached 1,614 entries in September 2026. The first half of 2026 brought roughly 167-178 further authorizations, depending on the count, so the 2025 pace is holding rather than accelerating. Outcome evidence is growing but modest: a JAMA multisite study found ambient scribes cut documentation time by about 16 minutes a day, roughly 10%, with larger gains concentrated among the 32% of heavy users.

Education and legal adoption has largely saturated at the individual level. HEPI's 2026 survey found 95% of UK undergraduates using AI and 94% using it for assessed work; 38% said their university now supplies AI tools. Pew found 54% of US teens had used chatbots for schoolwork, on a wider question than earlier waves. Gallup and Walton found 59% of K-12 educators using AI in 2025-26, a flat reading on a wider population. Clio reported 85% of legal professionals at firms with some AI adoption, up from 79%. The remaining questions in these sectors are about policy, assessment and verification, not uptake.

Spending and measured value remain the weak links in the industry picture. Gartner's September 2026 forecast puts worldwide AI spending at about $2.67 trillion this year, 56% of it infrastructure, but no public source updates IDC's industry split beyond 2024. McKinsey's 2026 survey found 89% of organizations using AI while only 37% reported any EBIT impact. Sector-level outcome measures are still mostly vendor claims or single-site studies. The exceptions are randomized or controlled studies in mammography, documentation and coding, and they show gains that are real but smaller and less uniform than adoption figures suggest.

takeaways_2026: Adoption ranks the same on every survey: Ramp (Aug 2026) puts technology at 80.9% and accommodation and food services at 33.1%; the Census Bureau (May 2026) puts information at 39.7% against a 19.8% national rate.

Healthcare is the fastest-moving regulated sector: 81% of US physicians used AI in early 2026 (AMA), and the FDA AI device list reached 1,614 entries in September 2026 after a record 335 authorizations in 2025.

Individual use has saturated in education and law (95% of UK undergraduates, HEPI 2026; 85% of legal professionals, Clio 2026), but institutional provision lags: only 38% of UK students say their university supplies AI tools.

Measured outcomes trail adoption: controlled studies show ambient scribes saving about 16 minutes a day (JAMA, 2026) and experienced developers working 19% slower with early-2025 tools (METR), while only 37% of organizations report any EBIT impact (McKinsey, 2026).
yoy_takeaways: Paid business adoption on Ramp rose from 36.4% (Nov 2024) to 46.6% (Dec 2025) to 55.9% (Sep 2026); finance and insurance moved from 51.2% to 58.1% to 73.7% (Aug 2026), the steepest climb among large sectors.

FDA AI device authorizations went from 235 (2024) to a record 335 (2025, contested range 295-335) to roughly 167-178 in January-June 2026; the cumulative list grew from 1,016 to 1,614 entries between December 2024 and September 2026.

Practitioner adoption converged at a high level: physicians from 66% (Nov 2024) to 81% (early 2026), UK undergraduates from 66% to 92% to 95% across three academic years, legal professionals from 79% to 79% to 85% (Clio).

The measures themselves changed: Census BTOS switched questions in November 2025, Pew widened its question from ChatGPT to all chatbots, Ramp expanded its sample in June 2026, and Gartner restated 2025 spending from $1.48T to about $1.79T, so several apparent jumps are partly definitional.

faq_2026.q: Which industry uses AI the most in 2026?
faq_2026.a: Information and technology businesses lead on every comparable survey. Ramp's AI Index showed 80.9% of technology firms on its platform paying for AI in August 2026, against 55.2% for all businesses, and the US Census Bureau found 39.7% of information-sector businesses using AI as of 3 May 2026, against a national rate of 19.8%. Finance and insurance is second on both (73.7% on Ramp; 33.9% on Census).

faq_2026.q: How many AI medical devices has the FDA authorized?
faq_2026.a: The FDA's AI-Enabled Medical Device List reached 1,614 entries in its 4 September 2026 update, covering decisions through 29 June 2026, up from 1,016 in December 2024. The September 2026 snapshot attributes a record 335 authorizations to 2025 and 235 to 2024; other counts of 2025 range from 295 to 333. Roughly three-quarters of all listed devices are in radiology.

faq_2026.q: What share of doctors use AI?
faq_2026.a: The American Medical Association found that 81% of US physicians used AI in their practice in a survey of 1,692 physicians fielded from 15 January to 2 February 2026, up from 66% in November 2024 and 38% in 2023. The average physician reported 2.3 use cases, most commonly summarizing research and drafting documentation.

faq_2026.q: Which industry spends the most on AI?
faq_2026.a: IDC ranked banking first, at about $31.3 billion of AI spending in 2024, with retail at about $25 billion and software and information services in the top three; together the three reached about $89.6 billion. For vertical generative-AI software, Menlo Ventures found healthcare largest at $1.5 billion in 2025, 43% of the $3.5 billion vertical total, ahead of legal at $650 million. No public source updates IDC's industry split for 2025 or 2026.

faq_2026.q: Is AI improving results in these industries?
faq_2026.a: Controlled evidence is limited and mixed. A JAMA multisite study published in April 2026 found ambient AI scribes cut clinicians' documentation time by about 16 minutes a day (about 10%); METR's July 2025 randomized trial found experienced open-source developers took 19% longer with early-2025 AI tools; and McKinsey's 2026 survey found only 37% of organizations reporting any EBIT impact from AI. Most sector-level gains published so far are vendor-reported.

stop_quoting.claim: The FDA has authorized about 1,250 AI medical devices (1,247).
stop_quoting.fact: 1,247 was the July 2025 list update. The list reached 1,614 entries in its 4 September 2026 update (decisions through 29 June 2026).

stop_quoting.claim: Gartner forecasts $2.59 trillion of AI spending in 2026, up 47% from about $1.5 trillion in 2025.
stop_quoting.fact: Gartner's 16 September 2026 forecast is about $2.67 trillion for 2026 (+49.5%), and it restated 2025 to about $1.79 trillion from the $1.48 trillion it published in September 2025. The figure is a forecast, not an outcome.

stop_quoting.claim: Generative-AI traffic to retail sites is up 1,300%.
stop_quoting.fact: +1,300% was the 2024 holiday season (Adobe). The 2025 holiday season was +693.4%, and the latest monthly reading, September 2026, was +71% year on year from a much larger base.

stop_quoting.claim: Teen use of ChatGPT for schoolwork doubled from 26% to 54%.
stop_quoting.fact: Pew's 26% (fall 2024) asked about ChatGPT only; the 54% (fall 2025) asks about any chatbot. The question changed, so the rise is not a like-for-like doubling.

stop_quoting.claim: Only about 5-10% of US businesses use AI, according to the Census Bureau.
stop_quoting.fact: That was the old BTOS question (AI used to produce goods or services). From November 2025 the Census asks about any business function, and the rate was 19.8% as of 3 May 2026; the two series are not comparable.

stop_quoting.claim: Only about 30% of lawyers use AI.
stop_quoting.fact: That figure (about 11% in 2023 to 30% in 2024) comes from a different survey series than Clio's, which found 79% of legal professionals using AI in 2024 and 85% reporting firm-level adoption in 2026. Cite the survey and its definition with the number.

gaps: Manufacturing has no three-year series: only Ramp's 61.1% of manufacturing firms paying for AI (Aug 2026) and Rockwell's estimate that 34% of operations are AI-augmented (May 2026). Eurostat's 2025 manufacturing share could not be verified (17.3% circulates but conflicts with Eurostat's statement that all sectors outside the top two were below 16% in 2024).
IDC's industry split is paywalled: no public 2025 or 2026 banking, retail or healthcare spending figure; Gartner does not split by industry.

Government: the 2026 federal AI use-case inventory is not yet published; no comparable state/local or non-US government adoption series was found. The 2025 federal count (3,611) is inflated by a reporting change.
Census BTOS sector rates were found only for information (39.7%), finance and insurance (33.9%) and retail (about 14%) as of May 2026; the 24.6% national reading for October 2026 is unverified.
Ramp's information-sector value for December 2025 was not found; Ramp expanded its sample in June 2026 and revises history, so earlier readings may move.
No AMA physician survey was fielded in 2025; no 2026 Menlo healthcare or enterprise vertical figures yet (expected December 2026); Eurostat 2026 data due December 2026.
FDA counts by year differ by snapshot and method (2025: 295-335; Q1 2026: 81 vs 92); FDA's own page could not be read, so all FDA figures are from third-party tabulations of the list.
Media and marketing has only the CMO Survey series; no newsroom or publisher AI adoption series was found.
Primary sites for Eurostat, the Census Bureau and FRED were unreachable from this environment; their figures are rated MEDIUM from consistent secondary reporting.
Clio's 2026 Legal Trends Report publication date is unconfirmed, and its 2026 wording ('some level of AI adoption at their firms') may differ from earlier years' individual-use question.

Site consistency: pages 863 and 938 still show 1,247 FDA devices; page 376 shows Gartner's superseded $2.59T and '2025 ~$1.5T'; page 865 labels Pew's 13% as 2023 (survey year) while this report files school surveys by academic year.
